mcqs.question: Why can a fast peripheral device still underperform even though the device itself is capable of high speed?
options: Fast devices always perform at their rated speed regardless of connection
The bus connecting the device to the CPU/memory has its own bandwidth ceiling, and the device can never exceed that ceiling regardless of its own capability
Device speed is determined entirely by the operating system's driver quality
Only storage devices, never GPUs or network cards, are affected by bus limitations
mcqs.explanation: The bus's own bandwidth is a hard ceiling independent of the device's raw capability. Devices don't automatically hit rated speed regardless of bus, driver quality is a separate factor, and bus limitations apply broadly across device types, not just storage.

mcqs.question: What two independent factors determine a PCIe link's total bandwidth?
options: The device manufacturer's brand and the cable length used
Lane count (how many parallel physical lanes) and generation (bandwidth per lane, which roughly doubles each generation)
The number of USB ports on the motherboard
The operating system version installed
mcqs.explanation: PCIe bandwidth scales with lane count and generation, independently of each other — a narrower link on a newer generation can match a wider link on an older one. Brand, cable length, USB port count, and OS version are unrelated to PCIe's own bandwidth math.

mcqs.question: Why does the total number of PCIe lanes a motherboard/CPU supports matter as a real system spec?
options: Because lane count only affects aesthetic labeling on the motherboard box
Because lane allocation is a finite, shared resource — giving more lanes to one device (like a GPU) genuinely leaves fewer available for other devices (like NVMe SSDs) at the same time
Because every device automatically gets its own unlimited number of lanes regardless of total count
Because lane count only matters for network cards, not storage or GPUs
mcqs.explanation: PCIe lanes are a finite budget that must be divided across all devices needing bandwidth simultaneously. This is a genuine hardware constraint, not cosmetic, devices don't get unlimited lanes, and the constraint applies across device types, not just networking.

mcqs.question: A PCIe 4.0-rated SSD is installed into a slot that only supports PCIe 3.0. What determines the actual achievable bandwidth?
options: The SSD's PCIe 4.0 rating always takes priority, so it runs at full PCIe 4.0 speed regardless of the slot
The link negotiates to the lower common denominator, so the connection is capped at PCIe 3.0 speeds despite the SSD's higher rating
The connection will simply fail to establish at all
The SSD automatically compresses data to compensate for the slower link
mcqs.explanation: PCIe links negotiate to the capability both ends support, so the slower generation caps the connection. The device's higher rating doesn't override the slot's limit, the connection still works (just slower), and there's no automatic compression mechanism at the link level.

mcqs.question: A user buys a top-rated NVMe SSD but measures far lower real-world throughput than advertised. What's a likely non-defect explanation?
options: NVMe SSDs never actually achieve their advertised speeds under any circumstances
The SSD may be connected via a narrower or older-generation PCIe link (e.g., x2 instead of x4, or PCIe 3.0 instead of 4.0) than the drive is rated for, capping real-world bandwidth
The SSD's rated speed only applies when running Linux, not other operating systems
NVMe drives require a firmware update every time they're installed in a new system
mcqs.explanation: A narrower/older PCIe link is the classic real-world explanation for underperforming NVMe drives, separate from any defect. Advertised speeds are achievable under the right conditions, OS choice isn't the determining factor here, and firmware updates aren't a mandatory step tied to bandwidth.
